title: Celibacy and married priests (CCC 1579–1580)
hook: Latin priests are usually celibate; Eastern Catholic churches ordain married men

segments.voice: Yesterday, three degrees: bishop, priest and deacon, one sacrament held three ways. Your line was three orders.

'Father, is that your wife?' A first-time visitor asks it at coffee hour, after the Divine Liturgy at an Eastern Catholic parish, and then wishes she hadn't. The priest just laughs: yes, and those are his three kids by the donut table. She had always assumed a Catholic priest couldn't be married. Across town, the Roman-rite pastor would tell her he promised celibacy at his ordination, and means to keep it. Both are Catholic priests, in full communion with the pope.
screen: `FATHER, IS THAT YOUR WIFE?` → `YES, AND THREE KIDS.` → `ACROSS TOWN, A CELIBATE PASTOR.`

segments.voice: Back on day one hundred thirty-one, you heard in passing that Eastern Catholic churches have married priests. Here's how that fits. The Catechism tells it as two disciplines, side by side. In the Latin Church, ordained ministers, except permanent deacons, are normally chosen from men of faith who live a celibate life and intend to stay celibate. Celibacy means not marrying, for the sake of the kingdom of God. The Catechism calls it a sign of new life, given over to the Lord and his people with an undivided heart, and points to Jesus's saying in Matthew about those who give up marriage for the kingdom of heaven. Then it turns east. In the Eastern Churches a different discipline has long been in force. Bishops are chosen only from celibates, but married men can be ordained deacons and priests. The Catechism calls this practice legitimate, and says these married priests bear real fruit in their communities. Celibacy is held in great honor in the East as well, and many priests there choose it freely. East and West, a man already ordained can no longer marry. The order matters: marriage first, then ordination. The Gospels hold both pictures. Jesus speaks of giving up marriage for the kingdom. And Peter, the rock, had a mother-in-law: Jesus healed her of a fever in Peter's house. Two disciplines, not two priesthoods, held in one communion. This week ran from the fruits of Communion, through conversion, penance, indulgences, anointing and Holy Orders, to today.
screen: `THE LATIN CHURCH: NORMALLY CELIBATE.` · `FOR THE SAKE OF THE KINGDOM.` · `THE EAST: MARRIED MEN ORDAINED.` · `PETER HAD A MOTHER-IN-LAW.`

segments.voice: A priest has a family too: parents who raised him, brothers and sisters, and for some a wife and children who share him with a whole parish. Picture one of those families, a mother waiting for a phone call, a child whose father is called out at dinner to a hospital. If you pray, ask God to bless them; if you don't, just hold them kindly in mind.

Celibacy. Not marrying, for the sake of the kingdom of God: the usual discipline for Latin priests, and the rule for bishops in the East, where married men may be ordained deacons and priests. Today's word.
Your line: two traditions. One Church, one communion, honoring both of them. That's the week.

chat.says: I met a married Catholic priest. Isn't that against the rules?
options: Not in the Eastern Churches: they can ordain married men as priests. Latin priests are normally celibate.
Yes. He must have left the Church, since every Catholic church forbids priests to have wives.
No. Any Catholic priest may marry after ordination now, as long as his bishop approves it.
chat.meaning: The Catechism describes two disciplines in one communion: Latin priests are normally celibate, while Eastern Churches ordain married men as deacons and priests. Bishops are celibate in both.

Divine Liturgy.meaning: the Eastern Churches' name for the Eucharist

Eastern Catholic.meaning: churches of Eastern tradition in full communion with the pope

Latin Church.meaning: the Western, Roman-rite part of the Catholic Church

full communion.meaning: complete unity in faith, sacraments and leadership

celibacy.meaning: not marrying, for the sake of the kingdom of God

notes: CCC 1579–1580 paraphrased (copyrighted translation). 'A different discipline has long been in force' follows CCC 1580's 'for many centuries', softened under the claims rule.
'Many priests there choose it freely' paraphrases CCC 1580's note that many priests in the East have freely chosen celibacy; confirm, or cut 'many'.
'Marriage first, then ordination' is the general Eastern practice; not stated in CCC 1580. Confirm.
'Celibacy is a discipline and a gift, not a rule written into the nature of the priesthood': a common way to put it; confirm phrasing for this path.
'The apostle Jesus called the rock' refers to Matthew 16:18.
